did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens by calling on all the earth to shout joyfully to God. From its very first verse, it presents praise as a universal matter, not merely a personal or national one.

Did you know? Alongside singing, the psalm also emphasizes honoring God's name: “Sing the glory of his name; give him glorious praise.” Praise is described as recognition of his greatness and exalted status.

Did you know? The psalmist does not merely call people to praise; he invites them to see for themselves what God has done: “Come and see the works of God.” In this way, praise is connected to reflecting on historical and human experience.

Did you know? The verse describes waters being turned into dry land and the people crossing the river on foot. This portrays God's control over nature and his ability to lead his people from danger to safety.

Did you know? The psalm presents God as ruling forever by his power, with his eyes watching the nations. Alongside its call for all peoples to bless him, it also contains a warning to the rebellious and arrogant.

Did you know? In the description of salvation, the psalm gives thanks for the preservation of life itself: “He has kept us alive.” Deliverance is also described as God not allowing our feet to slip—that is, not allowing us to fall or collapse.

Did you know? The trial is described through the image of refining silver: just as silver is purified in the furnace to test and cleanse it, so the people describe the hardships they endured under God's testing.

Did you know? The sequence of images in verses 10–12 describes a journey from hardship to relief: a fortress, distress, being made to pass over one's head, fire, and water—and finally the promise: “You brought us out to a place of abundance.”

Did you know? Beginning with this verse, the language shifts from a description in the plural to a personal description in the singular: the psalmist promises to come to God's house and fulfill the vows he made in a time of distress.

Did you know? The psalmist turns his experience of deliverance into a personal testimony and invites those who fear God to hear “what he has done for me.” The psalm concludes with thanks for a prayer that was heard and for steadfast love that was not withheld.
